title: Supervision 3 short-answer questions
description: Three short-answer questions (SAQs) on this week’s lectures. They’re for practice, not to hand in.
instructions:
Optional practice. These short-answer questions go with this week’s lectures. Only the essay needs to be handed in, but SAQs are good practice at writing short, focused answers, and they’re good revision too.

  • Each is marked out of five, so answer in bullet points and make at least five.
  • There’s no time limit, but about 10 minutes for each is a good aim.
  • For the graph in the first question, use Insert drawing (the pencil), or draw it on paper and add a photo of it with Insert picture.
  • Answer as many as you like. You can leave some blank and still submit.
  • After you submit, Review my answers shows you the points a good answer covers.

questions.title: Force, velocity and power
questions.text:
If you attach a 50 g mass to a muscle it takes longer to lift a given distance than a 5 g mass. Why does velocity decrease as force increases? Draw a graph to demonstrate the relationship. How does muscle power vary as a function of load?

Draw the graph with Insert drawing (the pencil).
questions.guidance:
• The graph. Plot the velocity of shortening against the force (the load). The curve falls from vmax with no load to zero at the isometric force, F0, and it’s concave upwards, a hyperbola (Hill, 1938). Label the axes and both intercepts, and draw the power on the same graph.
  • Why velocity falls as force rises. With no load, the filaments slide as fast as the cross-bridges can cycle, which depends on how fast the muscle’s myosin uses ATP. The load has to be borne by the cross-bridges that are attached, so the heavier it is, the more of them must be attached at any moment, and each spends more of its cycle attached and less of it detaching and moving on. The filaments slide more slowly. At F0 all the attached cross-bridges are needed just to hold the load, and there’s no shortening.
  • So the 50 g mass rises more slowly. The time to lift a mass through a given distance is the distance divided by the velocity. For a muscle that can just hold 100 g, Hill’s equation (with a = 0.25 F0) predicts that the 50 g mass takes nearly five times as long as the 5 g mass.
  • Power is force × velocity. It’s zero at both ends of the curve, with no load and at F0, and greatest at intermediate loads, at about a third of F0, where the velocity is about a third of vmax.
  • Beyond F0. If the load is greater than F0, the active muscle is stretched (an eccentric contraction), and it resists with more force than it can exert isometrically.
  • Why it matters. Muscles work best at intermediate loads, which is why the gears of a bicycle, and the levers of the skeleton, matter. Fast fibres, with faster myosin, have a higher maximum velocity and more power.

questions.title: Three diseases of muscle
questions.text: Relate the clinical signs with the physiology of: (a) malignant hyperthermia, (b) Duchenne’s muscular dystrophy, (c) myasthenia gravis.
questions.guidance:
• (a) Malignant hyperthermia is inherited (autosomal dominant), and most often caused by a mutation in the ryanodine receptor of skeletal muscle, RyR1. Volatile anaesthetics such as halothane, or the muscle relaxant suxamethonium, make the mutant receptor release Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum uncontrollably. The muscles contract (rigidity, often starting with spasm of the jaw muscles), and the SERCA pumps and the cross-bridges use ATP at a huge rate, so the body makes heat (a rapidly rising temperature) and CO2 (a rise in exhaled CO2 is often the first sign), with a fast heart rate and acidosis. Damaged fibres release K+, which can cause arrhythmias, as well as myoglobin and creatine kinase. It’s treated by stopping the trigger, cooling, and giving dantrolene, which reduces the release of Ca2+ through RyR1.
  • (b) Duchenne muscular dystrophy is X-linked recessive, so it affects boys. It’s caused by mutations in the gene for dystrophin, which links the actin cytoskeleton under the sarcolemma, through a complex of membrane proteins, to the extracellular matrix. Without it the membrane is torn by the forces of contraction, Ca2+ leaks in, and fibres die. Satellite cells regenerate them at first, but regeneration fails, and the muscle is replaced by fat and fibrous tissue. Signs appear in early childhood: difficulty running and climbing stairs, frequent falls, a waddling gait, Gowers’ sign (pushing up on the thighs with the hands to stand up, because the hip and thigh muscles are weak), enlarged calves (pseudohypertrophy, from fat and fibrous tissue), and a very high creatine kinase in the blood, leaked from damaged fibres. Most boys need a wheelchair by their early teens, and later the muscles of breathing and the heart, which needs dystrophin too, fail.
  • (c) Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease. Antibodies, most often against the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors of the neuromuscular junction, reduce the number of working receptors: they block them, cross-link them so that they’re taken into the cell, and bring in complement, which damages the postsynaptic membrane. End-plate potentials are smaller, so the safety factor falls and some fibres fail to reach threshold, especially as the release of acetylcholine runs down during repeated firing. The result is weakness that gets worse with use and through the day, and better with rest. It often starts in the muscles of the eyes, with drooping eyelids (ptosis) and double vision, and goes on to chewing, swallowing and speech, the limbs, and in a crisis the muscles of breathing. Anticholinesterases such as pyridostigmine help, by letting acetylcholine last longer in the cleft. The thymus is often abnormal, and removing it can help.
  • Connect each sign to the physiology. The best answers don’t just list the signs. They explain each one from the step that has failed: the transmission of excitation from nerve to muscle in myasthenia gravis, the release of Ca2+ in malignant hyperthermia, and the structure that holds the fibre together in Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

questions.title: Skeletal and smooth muscle
questions.text: Outline similarities and differences between the skeletal and smooth muscle contractile apparatus.
questions.guidance:
• The same motor. Both make force with myosin II (in different isoforms) pulling on actin filaments, by the same ATP-driven cross-bridge cycle, and in both the filaments slide past each other. Both are switched on by a rise in Ca2+ in the cytoplasm, and both have tropomyosin on their actin filaments.
  • Organisation. In skeletal muscle the filaments are arranged in sarcomeres, in register across each fibre, which gives the striations. Smooth muscle has no sarcomeres and no striations. Its bundles of actin and myosin run at an angle across the cell, anchored to dense bodies in the cytoplasm (the equivalent of Z discs, also containing α-actinin, and linked by intermediate filaments) and to adhesion plaques on the membrane, so the cell gets shorter and rounder as it contracts.
  • The cells. Skeletal muscle fibres are huge (up to 100 µm across and many centimetres long), with many nuclei at their edges, formed by the fusion of myoblasts. Smooth muscle cells are small spindles, a few micrometres across, each with one central nucleus, and in most tissues they’re linked by gap junctions into a unit that contracts together (unitary smooth muscle).
  • Regulation. Skeletal muscle is regulated on its thin filaments: Ca2+ binds troponin C, and tropomyosin moves to uncover the myosin-binding sites on actin. Smooth muscle has no troponin, and it’s regulated on its thick filaments: Ca2+ binds calmodulin, which activates myosin light-chain kinase, and phosphorylation of the regulatory light chain activates the myosin. Caldesmon and calponin, on the thin filaments, add another level of control.
  • Membranes and Ca2+. Skeletal muscle has T-tubules and an extensive sarcoplasmic reticulum, which meet at the triads. Smooth muscle has caveolae instead of T-tubules, and less sarcoplasmic reticulum, and much of its Ca2+ comes in from outside the cell.
  • Performance. Smooth muscle contracts more slowly, but it can hold its force for long periods using little ATP (latch bridges), and because it has no sarcomeres it can work over a much wider range of lengths, as the bladder and the gut must.
